journeyIntro: For making and keeping meaningful friendships. Learn to listen, show up and navigate changing needs.

steps.title: Someone has to go first
steps.body: Many friendships fade not because anyone stopped caring, but because both people waited for the other to get in touch. Going first is a gift.

steps.prompt: You haven’t seen a good friend for months and you miss them. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Wait for them to message first this time.
options.why: If they’re waiting too, the silence just keeps growing on both sides.

options.text: “I’ve missed you! Fancy a coffee next week?”
options.why: It’s warm, specific and easy to say yes to, with no blame about the gap.

options.text: “You never get in touch any more.”
options.why: Opening with blame can make them feel guilty rather than glad to hear from you.

steps.prompt: Make the invitation easy.
steps.before: I’ve missed you! Are you free for
steps.why: A small, low-pressure plan is easy to fit in, which makes a yes much more likely.

steps.prompt: What stops you reaching out to friends first?
steps.reply: Totally understandable. Most people are simply glad to be thought of.

steps.title: An old friend is back

lines.text: Guess who’s moved back to town for good! 🎉
Honestly, I barely know anyone here any more 😅

steps.prompt: What do you send back?

options.text: Nice! We should hang out sometime.
options.why: “Sometime” rarely turns into a plan, so they may stay just as lonely as before.

options.text: Oh cool, have fun settling in!
options.why: Friendly, but it misses the hint that they’d love some company.

options.text: Welcome back! Dinner this week? Thursday works for me.
options.why: You heard the hint and made a specific, easy plan, which is exactly how friendships restart.

steps.body: Send one warm, low-pressure invitation today to a friend you haven’t seen for a while.

lessons.title: Be Present
lessons.summary: Let a friend finish their story.

steps.title: The gift of full attention
steps.body: In a world of buzzing phones, simply listening to a friend without interrupting is rare. It tells them, more than words can, that they matter.

steps.prompt: Over coffee, a friend starts telling you about a really disappointing weekend. What’s the best response?

options.text: “Mine was even worse, listen to this.”
options.why: Swapping in your story moves the spotlight away just as they were opening up.

options.text: “Oh no, that sounds rough. What happened?”
options.why: It acknowledges the disappointment and invites the full story, so they feel heard.

options.text: “Look on the bright side, at least it’s Monday!”
options.why: Quick cheer-ups can feel like being hurried past a feeling they wanted to share.

steps.title: Let them finish
steps.body: Resist the urge to jump in with advice or your own story. Ask one more question than feels natural; friends often save the real part for last.

steps.prompt: Keep the story going.
steps.why: An open question keeps them talking and shows you’re interested in all of it.

steps.prompt: What makes it hardest to stay present when a friend talks?
steps.reply: Noticing it is the first step. Gently bring your attention back when you catch it.

steps.prompt: Present or distracted?

cards.text: Checking a text halfway through their story
Planning your reply while they talk

steps.why: Being present is mostly about small signals: eyes up, phone away and questions that follow their thread.

steps.body: Next time a friend shares something, give them two full minutes of attention before you say anything about yourself.

steps.title: Unsaid things grow
steps.body: When a friend keeps doing something that hurts, staying quiet can feel kinder. But small hurts that go unsaid often quietly end friendships.

steps.prompt: A friend has cancelled on you at the last minute three times this month. What do you say?

options.text: “I feel let down when plans change last minute. Can we plan something that suits you?”
options.why: It’s honest about the impact and moves towards a solution, not a verdict on them.

options.text: “Honestly, you’re a terrible friend.”
options.why: A label hurts and gets them defending themselves, so the real issue gets lost.

options.text: Say nothing and quietly stop inviting them.
options.why: They may never know why things changed, and you lose a friendship that could be saved.

steps.title: Feeling, then request
steps.body: Share how it felt, then what would help: “I was disappointed when Friday fell through. Could we pick a time that works better for you?”

steps.prompt: Share the feeling.
steps.why: Naming your feeling honestly gives them a chance to understand and make it right.

steps.prompt: Is there something you’ve been wanting to say to a friend? How could you put it?
Match each accusation with a fairer way to say it.

pairs.b: “I’d love to share my news too.”
“Can we pick a time that works?”

steps.why: Each rewrite swaps a label for a feeling or a request, which is much easier for a friend to hear and act on.

steps.body: Share one honest feeling with a friend, followed by a practical request, rather than letting it build up.

lessons.title: Keep Healthy Space
lessons.summary: Good friends can have different capacities.

steps.title: Always-on isn’t a duty
steps.body: Group chats and instant messages can make it feel like you owe friends constant availability. Healthy friendships have room for rest.

steps.prompt: It’s late, you’re exhausted, and a friend keeps messaging about their dating drama. What do you do?

options.text: Keep replying until 2am out of guilt.
options.why: You’ll be drained tomorrow, and tired replies help them less than a fresh conversation.

options.text: Mute them for good without saying anything.
options.why: Going silent without a word can feel like rejection and confuse the friendship.

options.text: “I’m wiped out and logging off. Tell me everything tomorrow?”
options.why: It’s honest about your limit and shows you still care about what they’re going through.

steps.prompt: Set a kind limit.
steps.before: I need to sleep now, but
steps.why: Pairing your limit with a plan to reconnect keeps the care obvious.

steps.prompt: Where do you most need space from friends?
steps.reply: Good to know. A small, kind limit there protects both your energy and the friendship.

steps.title: A big favour

lines.text: Huge favour… can you help me move flat on Saturday? 🙏
It’ll take all day, and you’re the only one with a car.

steps.prompt: Saturday is your only free day. Reply:

options.text: I can’t do all day, but I can drive the big stuff from 10 till 12. Would that help?
options.reaction: That would be amazing, thank you!
options.why: You offer real help within a limit you can keep, so you stay generous without burning out.

options.text: Ugh, fine. I’ll be there.
options.why: A reluctant yes often turns into resentment, and they won’t know you were stretched.

options.text: Sorry, I’m busy that day.
options.why: It isn’t quite true, and they lose help you could have given in a smaller way.

steps.body: Set one kind limit around your availability this week, and say when you’ll be around instead.

lessons.title: Follow Through
lessons.summary: Reliability is a quiet form of care.

steps.title: Showing up says a lot
steps.body: Turning up to the birthday, the gig, the hospital visit: these are the moments friends remember. Reliability quietly says, “You can count on me.”

steps.prompt: You said you’d come to your friend’s small art exhibition on Saturday. What’s the best way to handle it?

options.text: Forget, and hope they don’t notice you weren’t there.
options.why: They probably will notice, especially at a small event that means a lot to them.

options.text: Say “definitely!” without checking your plans.
options.why: Easy yeses that fall through hurt more than an honest “I’ll try, I’ll confirm Friday.”

options.text: Put it in your calendar now, and tell them early if anything changes.
options.why: Planning ahead makes it likely you’ll go, and an early heads-up respects their feelings.

steps.prompt: Be honest about plans.
steps.before: I’ve put it in my calendar, and I’ll
steps.why: An early heads-up gives them time to adjust and shows you take the plan seriously.

steps.prompt: When do you find it hardest to follow through for friends?
steps.reply: Knowing that helps you say yes more carefully, so your yeses can be trusted.

steps.prompt: A plan might fall through. Put these in order.
steps.why: Spotting it early and telling them quickly gives them time to adjust; a new time shows you still want to see them.

steps.body: Keep one promise to a friend this week, or let them know early and honestly if you can’t.

lessons.title: Handle Different Opinions
lessons.summary: Disagreement does not have to become distance.

steps.title: Different isn’t a threat
steps.body: Good friends don’t have to agree on everything. Handling differences kindly can actually make a friendship feel safer and deeper.

steps.prompt: Planning a group holiday, you want a quiet cottage; your friend wants a busy city break. What’s the best approach?

options.text: Insist on the cottage; it was your idea first.
options.why: Getting your way might mean a resentful friend on holiday, which isn’t much of a break.

options.text: Ask what each of you most wants from the trip, then look for something that fits both.
options.why: Understanding what sits behind each choice often reveals options you hadn’t thought of.

options.text: Agree to the city, then grumble the whole time.
options.why: Going along with it then complaining tends to sour the trip for everyone.

steps.title: Needs behind wants
steps.body: “Quiet cottage” might really mean “I need rest.” “City break” might mean “I want adventure.” A lively town by the sea could give you both.

steps.prompt: Ask about their reason.
words: really expect me to give up
steps.why: Asking about their needs, not their position, opens up solutions you both feel good about.

steps.prompt: In a disagreement, is it helpful?

cards.text: “What matters most to you about it?”
Looking for an option you’d both enjoy

steps.why: Helpful moves stay curious and honest; unhelpful ones put the person down or hide what you really think.

steps.body: Next time you and a friend want different things, ask what they most want from it before deciding together.

steps.title: Jokes can land badly
steps.body: Teasing is part of many friendships, until it touches something painful. When a joke hurts, how you respond matters more than the joke itself.

steps.prompt: In front of others, you joked about your friend’s break-up, and their face fell. What’s the best next step?

options.text: Later, privately: “That joke crossed a line. I’m sorry, I won’t do it again.”
options.why: It owns the hurt, promises change and respects their privacy by talking one to one.

options.text: “Come on, it was only a joke.”
options.why: It tells them their hurt isn’t valid, which can sting more than the joke did.

options.text: Tell the group they’re being oversensitive.
options.why: Talking about them to others adds embarrassment and can damage trust in the group.

steps.prompt: Own it simply.
steps.why: A simple, sincere apology is all that’s needed, with no defending or minimising.

steps.prompt: What usually stops you apologising to a friend?
steps.reply: All very human. A short apology costs little and keeps the friendship strong.

steps.prompt: Put the parts of a good apology in order.
steps.why: Naming the action and its impact first shows you understand, so the sorry and the promise feel real.

steps.body: If you’ve hurt a friend recently, own it in a sentence or two, without defending yourself.

lessons.title: Make Space for Change
lessons.summary: Friendships can adapt to new life seasons.

steps.title: Friendships have seasons
steps.body: Moves, new jobs, relationships and children change how often friends can meet. A friendship can stay close even when its rhythm changes.

steps.prompt: Your best friend has moved to another city for work, and your weekly pub nights have stopped. What helps most?

options.text: Assume they’ve moved on and stop messaging.
options.why: They’re likely missing you too; silence can turn a change into an ending.

options.text: Insist they come back every weekend like before.
options.why: Expecting the old routine adds guilt to an already big change in their life.

options.text: Suggest a regular video call and plan a visit for later in the year.
options.why: A new rhythm that fits the distance keeps the friendship going instead of letting it drift.

steps.title: Low effort, high warmth
steps.body: A voice note on your walk, a shared playlist, watching the same film over a call. Small, easy rituals can keep long-distance friends close.

steps.prompt: Which friendship has changed rhythm, and what new ritual could suit it?
Match each life change with a way to stay close.
steps.why: The best way to stay close fits the friend’s new life, rather than asking them to fit the old routine.

steps.body: Suggest one low-effort way to stay connected with a friend whose life has changed.

steps.title: Advice can wait
steps.body: When a friend shares a problem, our instinct is to fix it. But unasked-for advice can feel like “you’re doing it wrong”, even when it’s good advice.

steps.prompt: A friend vents about months of job hunting with no luck. What’s the most supportive response?

options.text: “That sounds so draining. Do you want ideas, or would a vent help more?”
options.why: It acknowledges the struggle and lets them choose the support they actually want.

options.text: Offer to rewrite their CV tonight.
options.why: Generous, but jumping straight to fixing can make them feel you think they’re failing.

options.text: “Maybe you’re just being too picky.”
options.why: It adds criticism when they’re already low, and they may stop sharing with you.

steps.prompt: Offer a choice of support.
steps.why: Giving them the choice respects that they know what they need right now.

steps.prompt: When a friend has a problem, what do you usually reach for?
steps.reply: Each has its moment. Asking first makes sure your support fits what they need.

steps.title: A hard night

lines.text: Jo and I broke up last night.
I keep going over everything in my head.

steps.prompt: What do you reply?

options.text: Honestly, you’re better off without them.
options.why: Judging the ex can make them feel they have to defend it, instead of feeling heard.

options.text: I’m so sorry. Do you want to talk it through, or a distraction tonight?
options.reaction: Can you come over? Company would really help 💛
options.why: You meet the hurt first, then let them choose what kind of support they need.

options.text: Download the apps and get back out there!
options.why: Rushing to the next step skips past a loss they’re still feeling.

steps.body: Next time a friend shares a problem, ask whether they want ideas or a listening ear before offering anything.

lessons.title: Celebrate Each Other
lessons.summary: Friendship makes room for mutual joy.

steps.title: How you respond to good news
steps.body: How friends react to our good news can matter as much as how they support us in hard times. Real enthusiasm says, “Your joy is safe with me.”

steps.prompt: A friend shares that they got a promotion, while you’re feeling stuck in your own job. What’s the best response?

options.text: Change the subject to how stuck you feel.
options.why: Your feelings are valid, but switching topics can make them regret sharing the news.

options.text: Congratulate them warmly and ask about it, then process your own feelings later.
options.why: They get the celebration they deserve, and your feelings still get attention, just separately.

options.text: “Lucky you, must be nice.”
options.why: A jokey dig can leave them unsure whether you’re happy for them, and cool the friendship.

steps.title: Mixed feelings are normal
steps.body: It’s human to feel a twinge of envy when a friend succeeds. You can feel it and still celebrate them. The twinge is about you, not them.

steps.prompt: Celebrate specifically.
steps.why: Specific praise shows you notice their effort, which makes celebration feel genuine.

steps.prompt: Celebrating or deflating?

cards.text: Turning to your own bad week
Sending a card or a little treat

steps.why: Celebrating keeps the spotlight on their joy; deflating shrinks it, even when that isn’t what you meant.

steps.body: Send one friend a specific message celebrating something they’ve done recently, big or small.
